text: 85 Guidance for national tuberculosis programmes on the management of tuberculosis in children l Provision of IPT as indicated. l Referral for CPT and ART as indicated. l Counselling on nutritional needs of infants or young children and other affected family members. l Health facilities should refer to and arrange for appointments with identified services and community resources before the family leaves the facility. Community support The usual approach to managing TB in children has been specialized care delivered at health care facilities. However, not all people with TB require referral for hospital-based investigations and care. Decentralization and delivery of care at the community level, when appropriate and available through an integration of family and child services, has the following advantages: l All family members requiring care for TB can receive them at the same time and in the same place. l Both time and money are saved when care is provided closer to home. l There is continuity of care between the patient’s home, community and local health centre. l Community support is increased, which may lead to better adherence to treatment and can be instrumental in overcoming barriers to long-term care, including treatment adherence, transportation costs, and loss of wages during sickness and clinic visits (13). It is also important to involve local schools, assisting them through education of the teachers and other staff about the needs of children with TB/HIV, the necessity for frequent visits to clinics and the importance of taking drugs regularly. This may help to reduce stigma in schools. Additionally, because not all children have the opportunity to attend school, faith-based organizations and other strong community groups could be involved in supporting children with TB and their families.
